title: Balanced Aerial Defence Starting Position
primarySkill: Establishing a balanced defensive starting position before an aerial contest.
objective: Develop a repeatable starting position that allows defenders to see the football, monitor their opponent and move efficiently into an aerial contest.
groundSize: One 10 x 8-metre channel for each group of three players.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge with one main teaching point
setup:
Mark a starting cone for the defender in the centre of each channel.
Position an attacker approximately 2 metres goal side of the defender.
Position a feeder 8–10 metres in front of the pair with a football.
The defender begins close enough to influence the attacker but without making contact.
The feeder uses hand signals or ball movement to direct the defender’s adjustment.
Create enough channels to keep waiting time minimal.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker stands still while the defender establishes a balanced starting position.
The defender positions slightly goal side, with knees flexed, weight through the middle of the feet and body opened sufficiently to see both the attacker and feeder.
The feeder moves the football from side to side or takes one or two steps laterally.
The defender adjusts with short, controlled steps while maintaining vision of both the football and opponent.
On the feeder’s call, the attacker moves one or two steps in any direction.
The defender mirrors the movement without crossing the feet or losing goal-side position.
No kick is delivered during the introductory repetitions.
Players rotate through defender, attacker and feeder roles after four to six repetitions.
coachingPoints: Begin close enough to influence the attacker without standing directly behind them.
Keep the feet approximately shoulder-width apart and avoid locking the knees.
Maintain a low, balanced position that permits movement in every direction.
Use peripheral vision rather than repeatedly turning the head away from the football.
Position slightly goal side unless the tactical situation requires otherwise.
Make small adjustment steps instead of leaning or reaching.
Keep the chest open to the football while maintaining awareness of the opponent.
Communicate early when working with another defender or goalkeeper.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the defender can see both the feeder and attacker before movement begins.
Whether the defender remains balanced rather than standing upright or flat-footed.
Whether the defender adjusts with short steps.
Whether goal-side position is preserved when the attacker moves.
Whether the defender turns completely towards the opponent and loses sight of the football.
Whether players understand the difference between close checking and illegal holding.

commonErrors.error: Defender stands directly behind the attacker.
commonErrors.correction: Move half a step to the side and open the body towards the football.

commonErrors.error: Defender stands upright with weight on the heels.
commonErrors.correction: Lower the hips, soften the knees and place weight through the middle of the feet.

commonErrors.error: Defender watches only the attacker.
commonErrors.correction: Use peripheral vision and maintain an open chest towards the feeder.

commonErrors.error: Defender watches only the football and loses the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Check the opponent’s position through body contact awareness and peripheral vision.

commonErrors.error: Defender crosses the feet when adjusting.
commonErrors.correction: Use short shuffle and drop steps to maintain balance.

commonErrors.error: Defender begins too far away to influence the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce the starting separation to approximately an arm’s length.

progressions: Allow the attacker to make longer leads within the channel.
Have the feeder deliver a gentle lob for the defender to track without contesting.
Add a second attacker so the defender must scan and identify the most dangerous player.
Introduce a second defender and require communication about responsibility.
Vary the defender’s starting position according to field location.
regressions: Keep the attacker stationary while the defender practises the stance.
Use visual floor markers to show the correct goal-side position.
Slow the attacker’s movement to walking pace.
Allow the defender to reset fully between each movement.
Remove the football and use the feeder’s pointing direction as the movement cue.
successIndicators: Establish a balanced stance before the attacker moves.
Maintain vision of both the football and opponent.
Preserve goal-side positioning during short movements.
Adjust without crossing their feet or losing balance.
Remain close enough to influence the eventual aerial contest.
matchApplication: The drill establishes the starting position required when defending a leading forward, resting midfielder or opponent positioned inside 50. A defender who can see both the football carrier and opponent is better prepared to judge the kick, close space, initiate legal bodywork and contest the football in the air.

title: Legal Bodywork Before the Ball Arrives
Emergency Double-Fist Spoil
primarySkill: Executing a controlled two-fist spoil when maximum distance is required.
objective: Teach defenders to use a safe and powerful two-fist spoil when the tactical priority is to create maximum distance from a dangerous aerial contest.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark distance zones at 5, 10 and 15 metres from the contest point.
Position a defender beneath or approaching the contest point.
A feeder stands 10–15 metres away.
A passive attacker provides a marking target during later repetitions.
The defender practises joining both fists safely before full-speed execution.
The football is delivered high enough to permit a balanced jump.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder delivers a high football towards the contest point.
The defender moves underneath the football and establishes balance.
The defender forms two closed fists with the thumbs positioned safely.
The fists are brought together to create a broad contact surface.
The defender jumps and drives both fists through the lower half of the football.
The football is directed away from the scoring area and towards the distance zones.
The defender lands with both feet balanced and follows the football.
One point is awarded for 5 metres of clearance, two points for 10 metres and three points for 15 metres or more.
Players rotate after five repetitions.
coachingPoints: Use two fists only when maximum distance is tactically required.
Join the fists securely without interlocking the fingers.
Keep both wrists straight.
Contact the lower half of the football to produce distance.
Extend through both shoulders and elbows.
Avoid swinging down towards an opponent’s head or arms.
Jump from directly underneath or slightly behind the ball.
Land with the feet underneath the body.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether both fists are formed safely.
Whether the fists remain connected at contact.
Whether the defender contacts the football cleanly.
Whether the spoil creates useful distance.

commonErrors.error: Fingers are interlocked.
commonErrors.correction: Form two separate fists and press them together.

commonErrors.error: Wrists collapse at contact.
commonErrors.correction: Align both wrists with the forearms.

commonErrors.error: Defender contacts the top of the football.
commonErrors.correction: Strike through the lower half to create distance.

commonErrors.error: Arms swing down towards the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Drive upwards and through the football.

commonErrors.error: Defender uses two fists when one hand would provide better direction.
commonErrors.correction: Reserve the technique for emergency clearance situations.

commonErrors.error: Defender lands heavily and cannot recover.
commonErrors.correction: Jump from balance and land with soft knees.

progressions: Add an active marking opponent.
Deliver footballs from different angles.
Require the clearance to avoid a central danger zone.
Add attacking ground-level players to punish short spoils.
Begin the defender from a moving approach.
regressions: Score only clean contact rather than distance.
successIndicators: Form a safe two-fist contact surface.
Direct the football away from the most dangerous area.
matchApplication: A two-fist spoil is appropriate when the football must be cleared from the goal square, the top of the goal square or another high-risk area. It should be used selectively because it creates distance but offers less directional precision than a one-handed spoil.

title: Wet-Football Aerial Defence
primarySkill: Defending an aerial football in wet or slippery conditions.
objective: Teach defenders to adjust positioning, decision making and aerial technique when a wet football is difficult to mark and likely to spill into a ground-level contest.
groundSize: A 20 x 15-metre area on a safe, stable surface.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Confirm that the training surface is safe and not excessively slippery.
Position one attacker, one defender and two ground-level support players.
Place a feeder 15 metres away.
Use a lightly damp football to create realistic handling difficulty.
Mark a boundary-side safe zone and a central danger zone.
Keep jumping and contact volume controlled.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder delivers a high wet football into the contest.
The defender assesses whether a mark can be secured safely.
When the mark is low percentage, the defender spoils or knocks the ball towards the safe side.
Ground-level players react to the likely spill.
The defender lands with reduced stride length and maintains balance.
The defensive team attempts to gather and exit through a boundary gate.
The attacking team attempts to win possession inside the danger zone.
Play continues for eight seconds.
Roles rotate after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: Expect the wet football to travel differently and slip through hands.
Allow additional space for the ball’s skid and carry.
Avoid low-percentage overhead marking attempts under pressure.
Use a firm fist rather than an open-handed slap.
Bring the football down towards defensive numbers when a long spoil is unavailable.
Keep the feet underneath the body on landing.
Anticipate a ground-level contest.
Communicate the spill direction early.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the defender adjusts to the wet football’s flight.
Whether risky marking attempts are reduced.
Whether the football is directed away from danger.
Whether support players anticipate the spill.

commonErrors.error: Defender attempts to mark every wet football.
commonErrors.correction: Spoil when pressure and ball condition make the mark unsafe.

commonErrors.error: Player uses an open hand and the ball slips through.
commonErrors.correction: Form a firm fist and contact through the football.

commonErrors.error: Defender lands with long unstable steps.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the landing steps and lower the centre of gravity.

commonErrors.error: Ground-level defenders wait for the spill.
commonErrors.correction: Move towards the likely drop area before contact.

commonErrors.error: Spoil drops into the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Direct the football towards boundary-side numbers.

commonErrors.error: Drill continues on an unsafe surface.
commonErrors.correction: Stop or modify the activity immediately.

progressions: Vary football wetness within safe limits.
Add a second attacker at ground level.
Begin from live wet-weather ball movement.
Require two disposals before the defensive exit.
Introduce repeated forward entries.
regressions: Stop after the initial ground-level gather.
successIndicators: Adjust decisions to the football’s condition.
Direct the likely spill towards support.
Win or pressure the ground-level contest.
matchApplication: Wet conditions increase spills, reduce marking reliability and create more ground-level contests. Defenders must prioritise safe outcomes, strong contact and immediate support around the drop zone.

title: Aerial Pressure and Contest Assessment
primarySkill: Assessing aerial-defence execution under pressure and contact.
objective: Assess each player’s ability to maintain legal, technically sound and tactically effective aerial defence across pressure, contact, fatigue and match-scenario conditions.
groundSize: One-third to one-half of an oval divided into five assessment stations.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Station 1 assesses balance through shoulder and late contact.
Station 2 assesses one-on-one mark-or-spoil decisions.
Station 3 assesses pack-entry lane selection and communication.
Station 4 assesses technique after fatigue or with a wet football.
Station 5 assesses repeat entries and scoreboard-pressure defence.
Divide players evenly across stations.
Assign a coach or experienced observer to each station.
Use consistent scoring for positioning, legality, decision quality, execution and recovery.
Modify contact and workload for age, injury status and conditioning level.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players begin at their allocated station.
Each player completes three to five assessed repetitions.
At Station 1, the defender receives controlled legal pressure before completing a spoil.
At Station 2, the defender enters a live one-on-one aerial contest and selects the appropriate action.
At Station 3, the defender judges whether to enter a pack aerially or protect the ground.
At Station 4, the defender completes an aerial action after a short running effort or with a wet football.
At Station 5, defenders complete a repeated-entry or late-match scenario.
Coaches record technical, tactical and behavioural scores.
Players receive one priority correction before repeating the station.
The assessment concludes with an individual aerial-pressure development target.
coachingPoints: Assess behaviour before, during and after the aerial contest.
Reward legal positioning and decision quality.
Penalise panic contact and unsafe pack entry.
Observe whether technique remains stable under fatigue.
Assess whether the player adapts to ball and weather conditions.
Judge whether spoil direction improves the defensive outcome.
Require communication in team situations.
Require an immediate recovery action.

commonErrors.error: Player prioritises physical contact over the football.
commonErrors.correction: Re-establish football tracking and legal contest position.

commonErrors.error: Defender uses the same aerial action in every scenario.
commonErrors.correction: Select the technique according to position, pressure and field context.

commonErrors.error: Pack entry is unsafe or unnecessary.
commonErrors.correction: Scan the lane and remain grounded when the aerial route is blocked.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue causes uncontrolled approaches.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce speed before contact and increase recovery between repetitions.

commonErrors.error: Wet conditions do not alter decision making.
commonErrors.correction: Expect spills and prioritise firm spoils and ground-level support.

commonErrors.error: Player stops after the initial contest.
commonErrors.correction: Require recovery, pressure or exit before the repetition is complete.

progressions: Combine all stations into a continuous match simulation.
Add positional role requirements.
Introduce live scoreboard changes.
Increase unpredictability of deliveries.
Repeat the assessment later in the chapter for comparison.
matchApplication: The assessment measures whether defenders can reproduce effective aerial defence when realistic pressure is added. Match performance depends on more than clean technical execution; players must maintain judgement, legality, communication and recovery under contact, fatigue and tactical consequence.

title: Intercept Defender Versus Leading Lane
primarySkill: Leaving an opponent to intercept or spoil a kick into a leading lane.
objective: Develop the defender’s ability to judge when to leave a direct opponent, attack an opposition leading lane and influence the aerial contest without exposing a greater threat.
groundSize: A 30 x 22-metre area with two marked leading lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position two attackers in separate leading lanes.
Match each attacker with a defender.
Place the feeder 20 metres away.
One defender starts closer to the likely passing lane and may leave the direct opponent.
Mark two defensive exit gates.
The feeder may kick to either attacker.
Defenders must communicate any release or cover action.
howTheDrillWorks:
Both attackers begin leading within their assigned lanes.
The feeder scans and chooses a target.
The defender nearest the passing lane assesses whether to intercept, spoil or remain with the direct opponent.
If the defender releases, the teammate adjusts to cover the exposed space.
The intercepting defender attacks the football from the side or front.
The defender marks or spoils towards support.
If the released attacker receives the football instead, the defenders must recover and delay.
Play continues for eight seconds.
The defending team scores for an intercept, effective spoil or controlled exit.
Players rotate after four phases.
coachingPoints: Scan the ball carrier and both attacking lanes.
Release only when the passing lane can genuinely be influenced.
Do not abandon a more dangerous opponent.
Communicate the release before crossing a teammate’s space.
Approach the football on a legal side-on line.
Attack the football at its highest reachable point.
If the intercept is unavailable, remain connected and delay.
Reassign opponents immediately after the contest.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the defender scans beyond the direct opponent.
Whether release decisions are based on the kick and field position.
Whether the teammate covers the vacated space.
Whether the intercepting line is legal.
Whether the defender arrives early enough to influence.
Whether the original opponent becomes a free scoring threat.
Whether defenders reconnect after the ball is spoiled.
Whether the aerial action leads to possession or safer territory.

commonErrors.error: Defender leaves before the kick is committed.
commonErrors.correction: Hold the direct opponent until the passing lane is confirmed.

commonErrors.error: Defender releases towards a low-value contest.
commonErrors.correction: Prioritise the most dangerous target and space.

commonErrors.error: Teammate does not cover the released opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate and adjust the defensive match-up immediately.

commonErrors.error: Defender enters front-on.
commonErrors.correction: Approach from a legal side or remain grounded.

commonErrors.error: Defender arrives late and creates contact only.
commonErrors.correction: Release earlier or stay with the direct opponent.

commonErrors.error: Defenders fail to reconnect.
commonErrors.correction: Identify the nearest dangerous opponent after the aerial action.

progressions: Add a third attacker and defender.
Allow attackers to exchange leading lanes.
Begin from live ball movement.
Add scoreboard and field-position consequences.
Continue into a full defensive transition.
regressions: Pause before the kick to check defensive positions.
successIndicators: Approach on a safe aerial line.
matchApplication: Intercept defenders create turnovers by leaving low-threat opponents and attacking predictable passing lanes. Poorly timed releases, however, can expose dangerous forwards, making judgement and communication essential.

title: Short-Hang Kick Contest
primarySkill: Defending a short aerial kick with limited flight time.
objective: Develop the defender’s ability to recognise a short, low-hang aerial kick, react immediately and reach the contest without losing control or conceding an infringement.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Position the attacker 8–10 metres from the feeder.
Place the defender 2–3 metres goal side or lateral to the attacker.
Mark a short-kick target zone.
The feeder varies between holding the football, using a handball fake and delivering a short aerial kick.
The attacker leads only when the feeder begins the disposal.
The defender must react to the actual kick.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder shapes to dispose of the football.
The attacker initiates a short lead.
The feeder delivers a low-hang kick into the target zone.
The defender reacts immediately and accelerates towards the drop point.
The defender shortens the final step before reaching the attacker.
The defender attempts to mark from the side or spoil with the nearest hand.
If the attacker marks, the defender applies immediate controlled pressure.
If the ball spills, both players continue for five seconds.
Players rotate after five repetitions.
coachingPoints: Recognise the short kick from the feeder’s ball drop and body shape.
React immediately rather than waiting to confirm the full flight.
Run towards the drop point.
Avoid approaching directly through the opponent’s back.
Control the final step despite the limited time.
Use the nearest arm.
Do not swing down onto the opponent’s hands.
Apply immediate pressure if the mark cannot be prevented.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: How quickly the defender recognises the short kick.
Whether the first movement is decisive.
Whether the defender takes a direct line.
Whether the defender contacts the football or opponent’s arms.
Whether pressure follows an unsuccessful contest.
Whether the defender gives up when late.
Whether the attacker receives uncontested possession.

commonErrors.error: Defender waits for the football to reach its highest point.
commonErrors.correction: React to the disposal cues and accelerate immediately.

commonErrors.error: Defender runs directly through the attacker.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust to arrive beside the opponent.

commonErrors.error: Defender reaches from too far away.
commonErrors.correction: Close the distance with the feet before extending the arm.

commonErrors.error: Defender swings down onto the hands.
commonErrors.correction: Reach through the football before it reaches the marking position.

commonErrors.error: Defender overruns the short kick.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the final step and lower the hips.

commonErrors.error: Defender stops after conceding the mark.
commonErrors.correction: Apply immediate legal pressure and close the next disposal.

progressions: Vary the kick between short, medium and fake deliveries.
Add a second short target.
Begin the defender further away.
Add a supporting defender and attacker.
Continue into a live possession chain.
successIndicators: Apply pressure when unable to spoil.
matchApplication: Short kicks into leading forwards or midfielders provide little time for defenders to respond. Early recognition and controlled closing can turn an uncontested possession into a spoil, pressured mark or immediate tackling opportunity.

title: Boundary Exit Aerial Press
primarySkill: Defending an opponent’s aerial exit down the boundary.
objective: Develop the defensive team’s ability to press a down-the-line aerial exit, contest the mark and keep the football trapped near the boundary.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a long boundary-side channel.
Create an exiting team and a pressing team.
Position one aerial target from each team near the boundary.
Position ground-level players inside and in front of the contest.
Place the exiting kicker at one end of the channel.
Mark two central escape gates for the exiting team.
The initial kick must travel at least 20 metres down the line.
howTheDrillWorks:
The exiting team prepares a down-the-line aerial kick.
The pressing team positions a defender on the corridor side of the target.
Supporting pressing players protect the front-and-centre and inside release.
The kick is delivered to the aerial contest.
The pressing defender attempts to mark or spoil towards the boundary.
If the ball reaches ground level, the pressing team attempts to force a stoppage or boundary result.
The exiting team attempts to gather and move through a central escape gate.
The pressing team scores for a mark, boundary result, stoppage or turnover.
The exiting team scores for a controlled central release.
Teams change roles after four to six entries.
coachingPoints: Position on the corridor side of the aerial target.
Force the contest towards the boundary.
Protect the front-and-centre spill.
Prevent the first clean handball back inside.
Keep one player on the feet to contain the exit.
Direct spoils down the line or over the boundary.
Avoid overcommitting multiple players aerially.
Reapply pressure after every incomplete possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the aerial defender protects the corridor side.
Whether support players position inside their opponents.
Whether the spoil is directed towards the boundary.
Whether an attacking crumber receives front-and-centre possession.
Whether the central release is closed.
Whether too many pressing players go to ground.
Whether the boundary is used as a defensive advantage.

commonErrors.error: Aerial defender starts boundary side.
commonErrors.correction: Move to the target’s corridor-side shoulder.

commonErrors.error: Supporting players stand behind the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the front-and-centre and inside spill.

commonErrors.error: Spoil returns towards the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Angle the contact towards the boundary.

commonErrors.error: All defenders attack the loose football.
commonErrors.correction: Keep one player on the feet to contain the exit.

commonErrors.error: Pressing team allows an easy handball inside.
commonErrors.correction: Close the first central receiver.

commonErrors.error: Defenders attempt a risky gather near the boundary.
commonErrors.correction: Accept the stoppage or boundary result when possession is unclear.

progressions: Allow the exiting team to use a short option before kicking long.
Add a second aerial target.
Remove the fixed boundary channel.
Begin from a kick-in.
Continue into a full-ground press.
successIndicators: Force boundary, stoppage or turnover outcomes.
matchApplication: Teams often exit defensive 50 with long kicks down the boundary. A coordinated aerial press can prevent the mark, trap the football near the line and create repeat attacking opportunities.

title: Team Aerial Structure Assessment
primarySkill: Assessing collective aerial-defence structure and role execution.
objective: Assess the team’s ability to maintain connected aerial coverage, assign contest roles and reorganise across varied team-defence scenarios.
groundSize: Approximately one-half to two-thirds of an oval.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Create attacking and defending teams with realistic positional numbers.
Mark a central corridor, boundary channels, deep-cover zone and defensive exit gates.
Position multiple feeders around the attacking half.
Prepare five assessed scenarios: long kick over the press, weak-side entry, central corridor entry, boundary exit and rebound entry.
Assign coaches to observe structure, communication, aerial role selection and post-contest recovery.
Use consistent scoring criteria for each scenario.
Adjust contact and running load for the playing group.
howTheDrillWorks:
The defence begins in its normal behind-the-ball structure.
The coach activates one of the five scenarios without announcing it in advance.
Defenders adjust line depth and spacing according to ball movement.
The defender with the strongest line claims the aerial contest.
Supporting defenders protect front, deep and weak-side spaces.
If the football is spoiled, defenders rotate according to its direction.
If the defence wins possession, it must complete a controlled exit.
If the exit fails, the coach may immediately activate a rebound entry.
Coaches score positioning, communication, aerial execution, support and reorganisation.
The assessment concludes with team and line-specific feedback.
coachingPoints: Assess the entire structure rather than the aerial contestant alone.
Maintain depth and width before the kick.
Shift collectively with ball movement.
Protect central and goal-side space.
Send one clear aerial contestant.
Maintain support in front and behind.
Use weak-side defenders intelligently.
Direct spoils towards defensive numbers or the boundary.
Rotate immediately after the aerial action.
Complete the defensive exit.

commonErrors.error: Team structure collapses around the football.
commonErrors.correction: Preserve front, deep and weak-side coverage.

commonErrors.error: Line depth does not reflect the kicker’s range.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust earlier according to pressure and kicking capacity.

commonErrors.error: Multiple defenders fly.
commonErrors.correction: Identify one contestant and assign support roles.

commonErrors.error: Weak-side defenders remain disconnected.
commonErrors.correction: Shift with the football and provide cover without leaving early.

commonErrors.error: Spoils return into central danger.
commonErrors.correction: Select the safe side before the contest.

commonErrors.error: Defenders fail to rotate after the spoil.
commonErrors.correction: Move the nearest player to the ball and cover behind immediately.

commonErrors.error: Failed exits create disorganised rebound defence.
commonErrors.correction: Recover goal side and rebuild the line before locating preferred opponents.

commonErrors.error: Communication becomes unclear under fatigue.
commonErrors.correction: Use short, agreed team calls.

progressions: Remove all marked zones.
Use fully live attacking transitions.
Add scoreboard and time-pressure scenarios.
Require repeated entries without coaching resets.
Expand into full-ground match simulation.
regressions: Assess one scenario at a time.
Pause during the football’s flight to review roles.
successIndicators: Adjust depth and width to ball movement.
Protect central, weak-side and deep space.
Support the contest at ground level.
Apply the team’s aerial-defence system across varied scenarios.
matchApplication: Team aerial defence depends on collective structure rather than isolated spoiling ability. The assessment measures whether the defensive unit can manage long kicks, switches, corridor entries, boundary contests and rebound phases while remaining connected and organised.

title: Deep Forward Match-Up and Goal-Line Support
Final-Quarter Repeat Entry Simulation
primarySkill: Sustaining team aerial defence through repeated final-quarter entries.
objective: Develop the defensive unit’s ability to maintain aerial technique, role discipline and structural connection during repeated high-pressure entries late in a match.
groundSize: Approximately one-half of an oval including defensive 50.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Create attacking and defending teams using realistic positional structures.
Set the scenario in the final quarter with the defending team under sustained pressure.
Position three feeders or attacking restart points around the forward half.
Mark boundary-side defensive exit gates.
The coach activates a new football after incomplete clearances.
Work periods should remain within safe match-like limits.
Provide full recovery and review between scenario blocks.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with an aerial entry.
Defenders organise the aerial contestant and ground-level coverage.
If the defence fails to complete a controlled exit, another entry begins immediately.
Entry location, height and target vary each time.
Defenders must recover shape while fatigued.
One defender attacks the football while teammates protect front, back and weak-side space.
The defence attempts to complete a two-disposal exit through a boundary gate.
The attack attempts to score or retain the football inside 50.
Each block lasts 45–75 seconds depending on the playing group.
Coaches score aerial role clarity, legal technique, ground-level support and exit quality.
Teams rotate after three to five blocks.
coachingPoints: Rebuild defensive shape while the next entry is developing.
Communicate roles despite fatigue and crowd noise.
Preserve one aerial contestant and organised ground coverage.
Control the final approach rather than crashing into contests.
Select the safe spoil direction before take-off.
Maintain a defender goal side or behind the contest.
Avoid rushed central exits.
Use clear leadership to organise tired players.
Stop the block if contact or landing technique becomes unsafe.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether defenders rebuild shape between entries.
Whether multiple players fly as fatigue increases.
Whether the deepest space is protected.

commonErrors.error: Defenders watch the previous contest.
commonErrors.correction: Locate the next entry point immediately.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue causes multiple defenders to fly.
commonErrors.correction: Re-establish one-up and supporting-ground roles.

commonErrors.error: Defender enters the contest uncontrolled.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the final steps and restore balance.

commonErrors.error: Deep cover disappears.
commonErrors.correction: Nominate a player to remain goal side.

commonErrors.error: Spoils return to opposition numbers.
commonErrors.correction: Identify the safe side during the kick’s flight.

commonErrors.error: Defensive exit is forced through the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Use boundary width and secure the first possession.

commonErrors.error: Communication becomes emotional and unclear.
commonErrors.correction: Use short, agreed team calls.

commonErrors.error: Work periods become unsafe.
commonErrors.correction: Stop the block and increase recovery.

progressions: Reduce recovery between blocks.
Add scoreboard and clock consequences.
Remove fixed feeder positions.
Use fully live repeat entries after turnovers.
Expand into a full-ground final-quarter simulation.
regressions: Limit each block to two entries.
successIndicators: Protect front, back and central space.
matchApplication: Final-quarter defensive periods often include repeat inside-50 entries with limited recovery. Strong teams preserve aerial role discipline and decision quality rather than allowing fatigue to create free kicks, poor spoils or structural collapse.

title: Position-Group Aerial Defence Assessment
primarySkill: Assessing aerial-defence performance according to positional role.
objective: Assess whether defenders can apply the aerial techniques, decisions and team responsibilities required by their specific match role.
groundSize: Approximately one-half of an oval divided into four position-specific assessment stations.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Station 1 assesses key defenders against leading and body-on-body forwards.
Station 2 assesses small defenders managing height mismatches and ground-level recovery.
Station 3 assesses intercept defenders releasing, covering and transitioning.
Station 4 assesses deep defenders coordinating goal-line and repeat-entry defence.
Allocate players according to normal or projected match roles.
Assign a coach or experienced observer to each station.
Use consistent scoring for positioning, judgement, legality, execution, communication and recovery.
Rotate players through secondary roles where appropriate.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players begin at their primary positional station.
Each player completes four to six assessed repetitions.
Key defenders manage varied one-on-one forward movements and deliveries.
Small defenders contest taller targets and must prevent clean marks or win the spill.
Intercept defenders decide when to release and how to cover behind the movement.
Deep defenders organise aerial and goal-line responsibilities.
Each station includes a ground-level continuation or defensive exit.
Coaches record scores and one priority correction.
Players repeat the task after feedback.
Selected players rotate to a secondary positional station.
The assessment concludes with individual and line-level development priorities.
coachingPoints: Assess players against the requirements of their position.
Reward correct decisions, not only successful outcomes.
Observe starting position before the kick.
Assess legal bodywork and approach safety.
Evaluate mark-or-spoil selection.
Judge whether spoil direction assists teammates.
Require communication in all support roles.
Assess ground-level recovery.
Assess whether defensive wins connect to an exit.
Identify transferable skills and role-specific limitations.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Starting position for the assigned role.

commonErrors.error: Every defender uses the same method regardless of role.
commonErrors.correction: Apply the positioning and decision priorities of the assigned position.

commonErrors.error: Player focuses only on winning the aerial football.
commonErrors.correction: Assess space protection, communication and the next possession.

commonErrors.error: Defender makes technically sound contact but directs it dangerously.
commonErrors.correction: Select a tactical spoil side before take-off.

commonErrors.error: Intercept defender releases without coverage.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate and confirm the rotation behind the movement.

commonErrors.error: Small defender relies only on jumping.
commonErrors.correction: Win position early and compete strongly at ground level.

commonErrors.error: Deep defender leaves the goal line unprotected.
commonErrors.correction: Balance aerial support with last-line responsibility.

progressions: Assess players against unfamiliar opponent types.
Remove station restrictions and use live positional play.
Add scoreboard and time pressure.
Include repeated entries at every station.
Compare results across multiple training blocks.
regressions: Assess technical and tactical components separately.
successIndicators: Connect defensive wins to team possession.
Demonstrate clear positional strengths and development needs.
matchApplication: Different defensive positions require different aerial priorities. Key defenders manage direct opponents, small defenders minimise mismatches, intercept defenders leave opponents to influence passing lanes and deep defenders protect the scoring line and organise support.
relatedDrills: SP-053 – Intercept Defender Versus Leading Lane
SP-072 – Deep Forward Match-Up and Goal-Line Support

title: Spoiling and Aerial Defence Chapter Final Assessment
primarySkill: Assessing complete spoiling and aerial-defence performance.
objective: Complete a comprehensive assessment of each player’s technical, tactical, positional and team-based aerial-defence capability across realistic Australian football situations.
groundSize: Approximately one-half to two-thirds of an oval, including defensive 50, boundary channels, corridor and goal square.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the assessment into five connected phases.
Phase 1 assesses individual starting position, approach, timing and spoil technique.
Phase 2 assesses live one-on-one contests from front, side and rear positions.
Phase 3 assesses two- and three-defender communication, aerial support and ground-level coverage.
Phase 4 assesses team structure against boundary, corridor, switch and deep entries.
Phase 5 assesses late-match repeat-entry defence and controlled exits.
Allocate players to appropriate positional roles.
Assign coaches to technical, tactical and structural observation responsibilities.
Use a consistent five-point assessment scale for each behaviour.
Modify jumping volume, contact and work duration for age, injury status and masters players.
Prepare emergency and safety procedures before beginning match-like phases.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete individual technique repetitions covering approach, jump timing, fist contact, arm selection and landing.
Players enter live one-on-one contests against varied opponent types.
Defenders are assessed on intercept, spoil and safe knockdown decisions.
Small groups complete aerial contests requiring one player to fly and others to protect the ground.
The assessment expands into team entries from the boundary, corridor and weak side.
Coaches activate high, short, floating and deep footballs.
Defenders must communicate roles, direct spoils and reorganise after the contest.
The team then completes a late-match scenario involving repeat entries and scoreboard pressure.
Defensive possession must be connected to a controlled exit.
Coaches record individual and unit-level scores throughout.
Players receive one final assessed repetition after targeted feedback.
The chapter assessment concludes only when every player has completed all required phases safely.
coachingPoints: Assess the complete sequence from starting position to the next possession.
Reward early positioning and flight judgement.
Require legal bodywork and safe approach angles.
Evaluate fist formation, wrist alignment, arm selection and contact point.
Assess whether players mark, spoil or delay according to position and pressure.
Judge spoil direction according to field position and teammate support.
Require an immediate second effort.
Assess communication before, during and after the contest.
Observe whether one defender flies and others protect the ground.
Assess line depth, weak-side support and central protection.
Require organised defensive exits.
Monitor technique and safety under fatigue.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Direction and distance of the spoil.

commonErrors.error: Defender focuses only on punching the football.
commonErrors.correction: Assess and coach positioning, decision making, direction and recovery as one sequence.

commonErrors.error: Player approaches too quickly and infringes.
commonErrors.correction: Close space early, then shorten the final steps.

commonErrors.error: Defender watches only the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Track the football while using peripheral and body awareness.

commonErrors.error: Player uses the preferred arm in every situation.
commonErrors.correction: Select the arm nearest the football and safe spoil side.

commonErrors.error: Defender attempts an intercept from a clear disadvantage.
commonErrors.correction: Prioritise preventing the mark and protecting dangerous space.

commonErrors.error: Spoil creates a second scoring opportunity.
commonErrors.correction: Direct the football towards the boundary, support or maximum safe distance.

commonErrors.error: Multiple defenders fly.
commonErrors.correction: Establish one aerial contestant and maintain ground-level coverage.

commonErrors.error: Defender stops after the spoil.
commonErrors.correction: Land, locate the football and complete the next action.

commonErrors.error: Team structure collapses around the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Retain front, deep, central and weak-side coverage.

commonErrors.error: Defensive possession is turned over immediately.
commonErrors.correction: Secure the first possession and use a supported exit.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue causes unsafe contact or landing.
commonErrors.correction: Stop the repetition, extend recovery and restore technical control.

progressions: Conduct the assessment without marked zones or predetermined entry points.
Use fully live attacking transition.
Add changing scoreboard and time scenarios.
Require defenders to operate in primary and secondary positions.
Compare scores with earlier chapter assessments.
Repeat the assessment during the season to measure retention and improvement.
regressions: Separate technical, contested and tactical phases across multiple sessions.
Use predictable hand-thrown or short-kick deliveries.
Assess younger players using foundation-level stations only.
successIndicators: Execute technically sound spoils with either arm.
Protect central, deep and weak-side space.
Connect defensive wins to controlled exits.
Maintain safe performance under pressure and fatigue.
matchApplication: The assessment reflects the full range of aerial-defence demands in Australian football. Players must defend direct opponents, support teammates, protect dangerous space, make risk-sensitive decisions, direct the football tactically and remain involved until the defensive team controls possession or safely ends the phase.
relatedDrills: SP-060 – Pressure and Contest Integration Game
